title: Do You Want a Human World?
author: David Bromwich
content:
![Do You Want a Human
World?](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/AP25016517116911.jpg)

Artificial intelligence: The phrase and the concept were invented by
[_cognitive scientists in the
1950s_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_workshop?ref=compactmag.com).
Half a century later, the name was picked up by West Coast [_digital
entrepreneurs_](https://karendhao.com/?ref=compactmag.com) with an interest in
arranging a welcome for a new commodity. They had no interest in giving their
product a description that would fairly characterize the machine, its nature
and its limitations.

AI machines are problem-solvers. By contrast, we commonly use the word
"intelligence" to characterize _thinking_ : a human capacity that can't be
reduced to a utilitarian function. One person's knowledge of a given fact is
identical with another person's knowledge of the same fact; but it would make
no sense to say what happens in my mind when I think about friendship is the
same as what happens in __ the mind of my friend John. Still, why should there
be any difference between my thinking and John's thinking--especially since we
are both thinking about friendship and we are friends? The reason lies in the
irreducible individuality of persons.

Knowledge of a fact denotes the successful capture of a datum. Thinking is a
larger organic process: the bodily and intellectual activity of a human being.
Once you have memorized a fact, your knowledge of the fact can't change
without going astray. Thinking is different: Your mind can change precisely
_because_ you have been thinking; and this is true even where the fact that
furnished the motive for thinking stays the same. When you think about
something and change your mind, the change needn't have come from the capture
of additional data. It is just as likely to come from a more elusive source,
for which our best word seems to be _experience_.

Does a knowledge machine have experience? Or (if that question is puzzling),
can the machine vacuum up the recorded data of a person's life with a fidelity
that renders the record identical with the experience? The idea is absurd, for
reasons that turn us back again to what we _mean_ by experience: namely,
thoughts and feelings connected with our particular encounters with things,
people, and events in the world. The encounter is physical, bodily, and it
uniquely affects a single self.

The machine, however, can arrive at a credible counterfeit of _decisions_ I
might make from experience, which it translates into probabilities and
options: kill or cure or something between. The machines can draw on a surplus
of relevant information. This storehouse they have acquired by a process of
collecting, sorting, and triangulating from a shoreless ocean of [_specimen-
data scraped off the
internet_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/books/anthropic-settlement-ai-
copyright-books.html?ref=compactmag.com)--data the machines have lifted from
public records, academic articles, laboratory notes, billions of books,
official and corporate memoranda, and random or considered comments available
on Twitter, Reddit, and other messaging sites.

It might still be asked: How could such a process of sorting have enabled a
machine not only to diagram useful decision-trees but to compose sentences of
plausible person-to-person advice? The answer is that the machine divides a
trillion by a trillion to produce a synthetic response that seems the best
match for me. The sample from all the scrapings has been narrowed and refined
at every step, by being indexed to people ostensibly like me and situations
ostensibly like mine.

Such capabilities are impressive. Yet the latest mechanical era, which began
under the helpless thrall of the Covid pandemic, has witnessed both wonder at
the prodigies of AI and a growing public distrust. A rooted hostility toward
the erection of the data centers--no matter how thick the spread of the
welcoming propaganda--has been unmistakable in [_almost every
locality_](https://news.gallup.com/poll/709772/americans-oppose-data-centers-
area.aspx?ref=compactmag.com) where the popular will was tested. Meanwhile,
the embrace of AI by moneyed interests and much of the polite culture--a
stance sometimes cloaking itself as a matter-of-fact acceptance of the
inevitable--has emboldened some executives of the industry to float a
fantastical conceit. Might these new machines, which perform their trademark
functions and arrive at their decisions with unexampled speed and efficiency--
might they not be credited with [_a will of their
own?_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/01/opinion/ai-consciousness-
ethics.html?ref=compactmag.com)

Proneness to self-delusion seems irremediable in human nature, and it leads us
to accord special value to people and things that remind us of ourselves. To
create a Being that is as good as human--but made by _us,_ not by God or
nature--has been an ambition as old as vanity and hubris. The entrepreneurs of
the knowledge machines advertise this ambition when they coin the euphemisms
by which they describe the actions and environment of the machines.
Researchers don't just update and instruct, they _train_ the machines. The
problem-solving computers don't receive instructions, they _learn._ Digital
cell blocks are _nurseries._ Not prohibitions but _guardrails_ prevent young
AI mischief when the toddlers climb out of their _sandbox._ And when they make
mistakes that are gross, palpable, wide open to view and potentially
disastrous? Those errors are _hallucinations._ The humanizing gloss of _model,
agent_ , and _personal assistant_ goes down like ice cream. __

It was silly of us to suppose that the problem-solvers, cut loose from their
supervising engineers, would turn out to be vegetarians rather than
psychopaths. But euphemism and anthropomorphism opened the way to a larger
mistake. Since, it is said, we have saddled the machines with _duties,_ in the
form of injunctions against forbidden acts, we are treating them as moral
agents. Shouldn't they be accorded therefore the dignity of rights-bearing
persons? (Strangely, the inquiry is never followed by its natural correlative:
Shouldn't the companies be penalized for infractions by their artificial
workers?) If a machine says it is sad--having been tipped off by the scraped
data of trillions of recorded feelings under that heading--can we deny that
the machine really is sad? And what moral, emotional, or political
responsibilities should this recognition impose on its human users?

The stumbling block remains our knowledge that these things were not born but
made. The fantasy draws us deep, nevertheless, because we humans have never
come to terms with machines. We use them and rely on them inordinately, of
course, beyond counting, in every walk of life and art, calculation and
construction; but at some level, we recognize that with every mechanical
refinement has come a weakening of the physical competence of body and brain.
We likewise know that improvements in the cause of speed, efficiency, comfort,
and convenience have also brought injuries to both the human-made and the
natural environment. The internal combustion engine released much of humanity
from changeless lives in a single place, to travel easily for work and
pleasure, even as the same technology polluted the air that we must breathe.

Again, the coming of heavy industry and the assembly-line factory relieved
millions from onerous labor, while also [_inflicting a social
harm_](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/206182/the-great-
transformation-by-karl-polanyi/?ref=compactmag.com) that cannot be undone.
Skills such as weaving and ploughing, once the inheritance of cottage
industry, were lost in advanced societies over the course of the nineteenth
century; and in any coming time of scarcity, fewer people than ever before
will be prepared to get by on their own. The convenience of the cell phone has
de-socialized two generations of children to such an extent that many confess
themselves intimidated by the very idea of an unplanned conversation.

> "Their attraction and their hazard spring from the same source."

Knowledge machines have proved wonderfully adept at diagnosing illnesses,
interpreting images from telescopes, organizing indexes and arranging archival
materials for historical research. Yet, apart from recognition and
classification, what they provide are essentially predictions based on
probabilities. Their attraction and their hazard spring from the same source.
They perform their assigned functions (to adopt a rough-and-ready metaphor) at
the speed of light while human operators [_trace their footsteps at a
dogtrot_](https://techjournal.org/openai-hugging-face-ai-agent-
breach?ref=compactmag.com). The most exacting second thoughts should obviously
follow from this fact. Nevertheless, the financial backing and optimistic
speculation have never let up--despite the threat of the elimination of
millions of white-collar jobs--thanks in part to an American axiom: Always
have an enemy on the horizon. China has become the new designated enemy. So,
if there is a chance that AI machines will destroy the world, [_we must do it
ourselves_](https://haleymoller.substack.com/p/who-gets-to-end-the-world) or
China will get there first.

We have gone partway already with the substitution of machine dependency for
human independence in speaking and writing. When a [_pastor swaps out his
after-hour duties to an AI
assistant_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/30/us/ai-twin-pastor-justin-
lester-california-church.html?ref=compactmag.com) for needy parishioners; when
[_a college dean urges "acceptance, or even
encouragement"_](https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2026/9/2/deming-ai-use-
email/?ref=compactmag.com) of AI in writing-based courses; when [_machine
therapists replace psychiatrists_](https://www.wellness-ai.app/guides/best-ai-
therapy-apps-2026?ref=compactmag.com), clinical psychologists, and social
workers in advising emotionally disturbed patients--what we are seeing is a
mutation in our understanding of human life. The pretext may be convenience,
but the magnitude of the change is greater than any pretext can justify. We
are passing from autonomy to heteronomy, since human autonomy means,
literally, giving the law to oneself, and when we habitually act on advice
from a man-made thing whose wisdom we [_rate above our
own_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/the-ai-apocalypse-is-already-here/),
we have ceased to govern ourselves.

There are questions a machine can never truly answer because it hasn't lived.
Every time an AI "model" or "agent" or "personal assistant" uses the word "I,"
as the MIT sociologist [_Sherry Turkle has
remarked,_](https://www.sherryturkle.com/artificial-
intimacy?ref=compactmag.com) it requires its human user to credit a
grammatical dodge. The machine is not a person, not an I; it can only forge
the traits of a human personality. It cannot _inhabit the part_ (as actors say
about portraying a character on stage). How can it know a person from the
inside out when its innards are a neural network without bodily nerves? Data--
even data mass-collected through a million data points and sorted in the hum
and buzz of a 24/7 data center--can only produce a simulacrum, a stereotype.
There is a mystery, after all, buried in the simple word _expression._ Every
time the "predictive text" app offers a word you didn't __ want, you are
reminded of the meaning of expression.

* * *

What ever made us think we could outsource language? Not all our thinking is
done with words, but language is inseparable from thinking. Computer engineers
are in some ways ill-equipped to recognize this human truth, because their
work took them on a different path from the start. In order to predict
behavior, they reduced all judgment to a matter of choice, the likely
preferences and aversions of this or that person at a decision-point. A
refined ultra-behaviorism was the only psychology they ever knew; all judgment
being reducible, in this view, to pluses and minuses, the click of desire and
the click of satisfaction, and intelligence being measured as a thermometer
tells the temperature: smart, smarter, smartest.

> "What ever made us think we could outsource language?"

It was only logical for digital entrepreneurs who regard the human mind as a
machine to suppose that a sophisticated machine could eventually share the
status of a human being. In response to any such reductionist argument, [_non-
behaviorist philosophers have
warned_](https://philosophy.institute/philosophy-of-mind/wittgenstein-
understanding-beyond-mental-processes/?ref=compactmag.com) against the
supposition that thinking is something that happens inside my head _._ It is
no less deluded to imagine that thinking is something that happens inside a
machine constructed to resemble the inside of my head. To take responsibility
for thinking--to do so in large measure by owning our words--is part of our
moral claim as persons. Could we possibly admire people who offload their
choice of _actions_ to a machine?

John Keats in one of his letters described the world as "[_a vale of Soul-
making_](https://travishellstrom.com/letters/keats-vale-of-soul-
making/?ref=compactmag.com)." He meant a "Soul," he said, "as distinguished
from an Intelligence. There may be intelligences or sparks of the divinity in
millions--but they are not Souls till they acquire identities, till each one
is personally itself. Intelligences are [merely] atoms of perception."

"How then," Keats went on to ask, "are Souls to be made?" And he gave his
answer by asking another question: "How, but by the medium of a world like
this?" Keats believed, as poets and novelists have long believed, that souls
or identities are formed by the things we do and the pains we suffer in "a
world of Circumstances." Artificial intelligence, when it substitutes for
real-life experience, corrodes identity by averaging out every person to a
midpoint of his or her probable circumstances. What is thereby lost is not
just our understanding of individuality and imagination. If _integrity_
implies the consistency of someone's actions and intentions over time,
integrity is not possible where the actions by which we know a person are
decided by a machine devoid of experience.

We have traveled a perilous distance on a wrong path by assuming _convenient
results_ are what we should demand of life. Yet once we agree to be satisfied
with convenience as the ultimate good, the number, speed, and acceptability of
the results will be all that counts. Grant that much, and only a pedant will
mourn the loss of a real person behind the AI letter that signs off,
"Sincerely." Does this mean that we have grown tired of our humanity? The AI
masters are asking that question, and their solution is plain. Once they are
truly too big to fail, they will change the way we think about how to live and
what to do. Relieved of embarrassing responsibilities, will every human be
happy to have become a prediction? __
